title: “Every New Day Is a Gift”: Heart Transplantation beyond 70 Years—From Chronological Age to Biological Reserve and the Patient Perspective
content:
Heart transplantation has evolved from an experimental procedure performed mainly in younger patients into an established treatment for selected individuals with advanced heart failure. One important change has been the declining role of chronological age as an isolated criterion for transplant candidacy. Historical experience, together with advances in immunosuppression, surgical techniques, perioperative care, and patient selection, has shown that carefully selected patients in their seventh decade can achieve favorable outcomes after transplantation. Contemporary guidelines recommend a multidimensional assessment that considers comorbidities, functional status, frailty, organ function, nutritional status, cognitive and psychosocial factors, and the potential for postoperative recovery and rehabilitation. Recent registry data indicate that heart transplantation is increasingly being performed in patients aged ≥70 years and can be associated with favorable outcomes, although these recipients remain a highly selected population.
This narrative review summarizes the historical evolution of age criteria in heart transplantation, the evidence concerning recipients aged ≥70 years, and the growing importance of biological and functional reserve in transplant evaluation. Particular attention is paid to frailty as a multidimensional geriatric condition rather than simply a consequence of chronological age.
The review is complemented by the perspective of Umberto, a 72-year-old man who recently underwent heart transplantation. His experience illustrates the emotional, functional, and social dimensions of transplantation in later life and provides a patient-centered perspective on the geriatric principle that chronological age should be interpreted in the context of biological reserve, resilience, and individual potential for recovery.
